nameStory: This sea star is named after Edward Forbes, a 19th-century British naturalist who was a pioneer in marine biology and ocean exploration. Forbes revolutionized our understanding of sea life by studying creatures at different ocean depths, making him a fitting namesake for this common coastal starfish. His work helped establish the field of marine ecology that we know today.
description: Forbes's Sea Star is a classic five-armed starfish that embodies what most people picture when they think of a sea star. These sturdy marine animals typically measure 3-5 inches across when fully grown, with thick, fleshy arms radiating from a central disc. Their upper surface is covered in small, bumpy plates that give them a rough, pebbly texture, while their underside features hundreds of tiny tube feet used for movement and feeding. They come in various colors, most commonly orange, purple, or reddish-brown.

idTips.label: Five thick arms
idTips.description: Always has exactly five arms that are broad and sturdy, not thin or delicate - they feel substantial and meaty when gently touched

idTips.label: Bumpy upper surface
idTips.description: Top side feels like coarse sandpaper with small, hard bumps and plates - run your finger gently across it for a distinctly rough, irregular texture

idTips.label: Tube feet underneath
idTips.description: Flip it over to see hundreds of small, pale tube feet along grooves on each arm - they feel soft and slightly sticky to the touch

idTips.label: Variable coloring
idTips.description: Most commonly orange, purple, or reddish-brown, but can be yellow or even pale - color alone isn't reliable for identification

idTips.label: Flexible arms
idTips.description: Arms can bend and curl considerably - if you gently lift one arm, it will flex and wrap slightly around your finger

idTips.label: Central disc
idTips.description: Body has a distinct central disc that's clearly separate from the arms, rather than arms that gradually merge into the center

habitat: Forbes's Sea Stars live in shallow coastal waters along New England's rocky shores, tide pools, and sandy or muddy bottoms. You'll find them from the low tide line down to about 900 feet deep, often clinging to rocks, shells, or pier pilings. They're particularly common in protected bays and harbors where they hunt for mussels, clams, and other shellfish.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm up, moving into shallower areas and beginning their peak feeding season on shellfish beds.
seasonality.summer: Easily found in tide pools and shallow water during low tides - this is the best time for observation and identification.
seasonality.fall: Still active and visible, often moving to slightly deeper waters as temperatures begin to cool.
seasonality.winter: Present but less active in deeper waters, rarely seen in tide pools during this dormant period.

funFact: Forbes's Sea Stars can actually push their stomach outside their body to digest prey too large to fit in their mouth - they envelope a clam or mussel, pry it open with their arms, then insert their stomach through the tiny gap to dissolve the soft tissue inside before pulling their stomach back in!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the Common Sea Star (Asterias rubens), but Forbes's tends to be more orange or reddish while Common Sea Stars are usually more purple or violet. Memory trick: Forbes likes 'fiery' colors (orange/red) while Common prefers 'cool' colors (purple/violet).
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'starfish,' these animals are not fish at all - they're echinoderms, more closely related to sea urchins and sand dollars. The preferred term 'sea star' better reflects their true nature as marine invertebrates with radial symmetry and a unique water-based circulatory system.
compareHints: Forbes's Sea Star differs from its close relative, the Common Sea Star, primarily in color preference and habitat. Forbes's tends toward warmer colors (orange, red, brown) and prefers slightly warmer, more protected waters, while Common Sea Stars favor cooler purples and violets and tolerate more exposed, colder conditions. Both have the same basic five-armed structure and bumpy texture, making color and location your best distinguishing clues.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The common sea star differs from its close relative Forbes's sea star primarily in texture and color.
